statement: How many of the whole numbers from 1 to 1000 are divisible by neither 6 nor 15?

choices.misconception: I counted the numbers divisible by 6 or by 15 correctly but forgot that the question asks for those divisible by neither.
I removed the 166 multiples of 6 and the 66 multiples of 15 but did not add back the numbers I had removed twice.
I added back the multiples of 6 x 15 = 90 instead of the multiples of the least common multiple, 30.
I removed only the multiples of 6 and forgot about the multiples of 15.

hints: Count the numbers you must remove first.

Use inclusion-exclusion: multiples of 6 plus multiples of 15, minus the numbers that are multiples of both. A number is a multiple of both exactly when it is a multiple of their least common multiple.
There are 166 multiples of 6 and 66 multiples of 15 up to 1000, and the least common multiple of 6 and 15 is 30.

solutions.reliable: Up to 1000 there are 166 multiples of 6 and 66 multiples of 15. The numbers that are multiples of both are the multiples of 30, and there are 33 of them. So 166 + 66 - 33 = 199 numbers are divisible by 6 or 15, and 1000 - 199 = 801 are divisible by neither. The transferable idea: in inclusion-exclusion the overlap is the multiples of the least common multiple, not of the product.
solutions.elegant: Work in blocks of 30. From 1 to 30 the multiples of 6 or 15 are 6, 12, 15, 18, 24 and 30, so 24 of every 30 numbers survive. The 33 full blocks up to 990 give 33 x 24 = 792, and from 991 to 1000 only 996 is removed, leaving 9 more. Total 801.

whyOnTest: Two-set inclusion-exclusion with a non-obvious overlap: numbers divisible by both are set by the least common multiple, 30, not by 6 x 15 = 90.
